clavicular-s-looksmaxxing-philosophy.summary: Streamer Clavicular's all-in 'ascension' approach, which pairs drugs, extreme dieting and bonesmashing talk with the goal of a sharper face and physique.

quick.overview:
Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Peters, an American streamer who became prominent in 2025 and 2026 on Kick and TikTok. His approach, called 'hardmaxxing' by followers, is a maximal template for 'ascension': a sharper face, a leaner physique and a more commanding presence.

The chain runs through an aggressive mindset, then anabolic steroids, injectable peptides, extreme dieting and bonesmashing, aimed at changing face and body. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources describe bonesmashing as pseudoscientific.
quick.how: Followers treat the approach as a package: streams and clips for the mindset, a paid course that includes guides on injectable peptides, and a mix of drug use, strict dieting and physical modification. People combine it with standard looksmaxxing steps such as fitness and skincare, and results are described over months to years.
quick.risks: Critics, including doctors, argue the content harms young men, and bonesmashing is described by medical sources as dangerous. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says he overdosed on a livestream in 2026 after a five-drug 'pentastack'. Legal matters reported include arrests, some with charges dropped, and a September 2026 Massachusetts charge that he denies and which remains an allegation.

angle.text: Followers of streamer Clavicular use his approach as a template for maximal 'ascension': an aggressive mindset plus drug protocols, bonesmashing talk and extreme self-improvement aimed at a more striking face and physique. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources have criticised the approach.

looksmax-org-forum-participation.summary: The main forum hub of looksmaxxing, where members post progress photos, get PSL ratings and swap guides for improving face and body.

quick.overview:
Looksmax.org is described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing, alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com. Members post photos for feedback, ask for ratings and share guides, using the replies as a map for what to improve in their face and body.

The chain is simple: post photos, get a current and 'potential' PSL score from peers, read the shared guides, then apply tips on skin, grooming, fitness or procedures. The feedback comes from peers on a self-devised rating scale, and the guides' methods range from studied to anecdotal.
quick.how: Members typically post front and side photos, discuss softmaxxing (non-invasive changes) and hardmaxxing (surgery, steroids), and use shared vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes. Many post progress photos over months to track changes. Anonymity is common.
quick.risks: Commentators and researchers link the subculture to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety, promotion of dangerous methods, blackpill determinism and radicalisation. Critics also call the PSL scale unscientific and biased against non-white men. Members often gatekeep against casual 'normies'.

angle.text: Members post progress photos, request ratings and swap guides, using the feedback and shared methods as a map for improving face and body. The ratings come from peers on a self-devised scale, and the guides' methods vary from studied to anecdotal.

dopamine-porn-avoidance.summary: Abstaining from porn, masturbation or other stimulation, popular in self-improvement circles, with the aim of more drive, focus and confidence.

quick.overview:
This practice covers avoiding pornography, masturbation and other highly stimulating habits. Followers of NoFap and 'dopamine fasting' do it hoping for higher testosterone, focus and confidence, which they say makes a person come across as more attractive and present.

The chain proponents describe is: abstain, reward system 'resets', more drive and willpower, more confidence. Researchers describe the specific hormone and appearance claims as unsupported. Dopamine fasting itself was developed by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a behavioural tool to reduce impulsive behaviours, not to literally lower dopamine.
quick.how: In looksmaxxing circles abstaining is listed as a free step alongside fitness and skincare. People track streaks in communities such as NoFap, and dopamine fasting versions cut out phones, snacks or other high-stimulation habits for set periods. Users report changes in focus and mood over weeks.
quick.risks: Surveys found members' mental health problems were more plausibly linked to underlying disorders than to abstinence, and some researchers argue prolonged abstinence may worsen distress. Extreme versions such as sensory deprivation are criticised by clinicians. DSM-5-TR does not recognise porn addiction.

angle.text: Followers of NoFap and dopamine fasting abstain hoping to raise drive, focus and confidence, which they say makes a person come across as more attractive. Researchers describe the hormone and appearance claims as unsupported, though dopamine fasting was developed as a behavioural tool.

alpha-sigma-male-frameworks.summary: Informal alpha, beta and sigma ranking of men; users adopt the high-status archetypes to act more assertively and seem more attractive.

quick.overview:
Alpha, beta and sigma are labels online men's communities use to rank men by perceived dominance and status. 'Alpha' is dominant and high-status, 'beta' deferential, and 'sigma' a solitary high-status 'lone wolf', now often used ironically.

The appeal is the chain: adopt a high-status identity, act with more assertiveness, and be read as higher status and more attractive. The terms were borrowed from animal-behaviour research and popularised by media and pickup-artist books from the 1990s and 2000s; researchers describe applying them to humans as an oversimplification.
quick.how: The frameworks are labels rather than methods. Users take on the archetype's behaviours, such as assertiveness, composure and self-reliance, and combine it with looks, frame and status building discussed in the same forums.
quick.risks: Researchers say studies of human attraction emphasise prestige and warmth more than dominance. The labels are sometimes used pejoratively within manosphere communities, and the framework is often tied to manosphere ideology.

angle.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing forum users sort men into alpha, beta and sigma types and adopt the high-status archetypes to act more assertively and seem more attractive. The typology is borrowed from animal-behaviour research and is not an established model of human social life.

social-proof-status-maxxing.summary: Building visible signals of approval and rank, such as followers, friends and high-status associations, so others see you as higher status and more attractive.

quick.overview:
Social proof and status maxxing mean showing signs of other people's approval and rank, such as friends, followers, group photos and associations, so you come across as higher status and more attractive.

The chain: visible approval signals, then others read you as higher status, then you seem more attractive overall. Social proof, a term coined by Robert Cialdini in 1984, is a well-documented tendency to copy others' cues when unsure. Whether the specific looksmaxxing tactics change dating or career outcomes has not been tested directly.
quick.how: People build a social presence: group photos, an active friend circle, followers, endorsements and time around high-status people. It is usually done alongside improving looks, grooming and style, and builds over months.
quick.risks: No medical risks. Effects depend on context and culture, and research notes social proof often produces compliance without private belief.

angle.text: Users build visible signals such as followers, group photos and high-status associations so others read them as higher status and more attractive. The psychology of social proof is well studied; the looksmaxxing tactics built on it have not been tested directly.

money-maxxing-career-maxxing.summary: Raising income and career standing to gain status and resources that can offset or outweigh looks in dating, and fund appearance upgrades.

quick.overview:
Money maxxing and career maxxing mean pursuing income and professional success as a route to status and attractiveness, especially for men who see their looks as fixed.

The chain: higher income and career standing give status and resources, which raise perceived desirability and also pay for grooming, clothes, skincare and procedures. Evolutionary-psychology research reports that mate preferences track status and resources, and one cited study found higher-salaried men rated more attractive. Research also links perceived attractiveness to employment outcomes.
quick.how: People pursue promotions, higher-paying skills, businesses or investing, then spend part of the gains on appearance. It runs alongside or instead of looks work and plays out over years.
quick.risks: No direct health risks. Outcomes vary by person and culture, and the research findings are correlational.

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and manosphere communities present income and career success as a route to attractiveness: status and resources raise desirability and also pay for appearance upgrades. Mate-preference research partly supports a link between status and desirability.

smile-practice-smile-maxxing.summary: Rehearsing your smile in a mirror so it looks more genuine, symmetrical and warm, which makes your face come across as more likable.

quick.overview:
Smile maxxing means practising and refining your smile, usually in a mirror, so it looks more natural, symmetrical and warm.

The chain: rehearse the smile, get a more genuine and even expression, and your face reads as warmer and more approachable. Research distinguishes the Duchenne smile, which engages the muscle around the eyes, from the voluntary 'Pan Am' smile using only the mouth, and studies report smiling makes people seem more likable. Smile training itself has not been studied.
quick.how: People practise in a mirror or on camera, aiming to use the muscles around the eyes as well as the mouth, and check which side and amount of teeth look best. It is a free daily habit often paired with teeth whitening or orthodontics. Facial feedback research suggests expressions may slightly affect mood; a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small effects.
quick.risks: No medical risks reported. Cultural context affects how smiles are read.

angle.text: Users rehearse their smile in a mirror so it looks more genuine and symmetrical, drawing on the difference between polite and genuine smiles. Studies show smiles make people seem more likable; smile training itself has not been studied.

posture-frame-body-language.summary: Standing upright with an open, expansive stance so you look taller and broader and come across as more confident.

quick.overview:
Posture, frame and body language practices use an upright, open and expansive stance so you look taller, broader and more confident while standing and moving. The visual change is immediate.

The chain: open posture gives a taller, broader impression, which makes you look and feel more confident. Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel; the hormonal and behavioural effects reported for power posing in 2010 have not replicated well, and reviews find a reliable effect on feelings of power but not physiology.
quick.how: People practise standing tall with shoulders back, an open chest and head level, and use power poses before events. It is combined with back and core training and is a free habit that can show in photos right away.
quick.risks: No direct risks reported. There is ongoing disagreement about effect sizes for the feeling-of-power research.

angle.text: Users hold an upright, open stance, sometimes as power posing, so they look taller, broader and more confident while standing. The visual change is immediate; hormone and behaviour claims from posing have replicated poorly, while effects on how people feel are better supported.

photo-comparison-flip-test.summary: Comparing a photo with its flipped mirror image to see which version looks better and pick more flattering angles and framing.

quick.overview:
The flip test means comparing your photo with a horizontally flipped copy, or with your mirror image, to understand why you look different in pictures and which version looks better.

The chain: compare the versions, notice which side or look is more flattering, then choose angles and framing accordingly. Users say familiarity with the mirror image shapes preference, which relates to the mere-exposure effect, first studied by Zajonc in 1968. No studies have tested the practice itself.
quick.how: People flip selfies in a photo app, view them beside the originals and pick the version or angle they prefer for profiles and posts. It takes minutes and is often repeated across several photos.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Some community members report distress from close self-scrutiny.

angle.text: Users flip photos or compare them with their mirror image to understand why they look different in pictures and to pick the more flattering version and angle. It relates to the mere-exposure effect, though the method itself has not been tested.

mirror-flip-symmetry-test.summary: Flipping a face photo or splitting it into halves to check left-right symmetry and pick flattering angles or features to work on.

quick.overview:
The mirror flip test compares a face photo with its left-right reversed copy, or builds composites from each half of the face, to see how symmetrical it looks. It is a common self-check in facial-analysis content.

The chain: flip or split the photo, judge left-right differences, then target asymmetries or choose angles. Research treats symmetry as one of three factors, with averageness and youthfulness, in attractiveness judgments; studies from the 1990s and 2000s found symmetrical faces tend to be rated as more attractive, with a larger effect for female faces. No published study has evaluated the test itself.
quick.how: People reverse a photo horizontally or build left-left and right-right composites in a photo app and compare them with the original, looking at eyes, brows, jaw and nose. Results are used to choose which side to show or what to address with grooming, hair or procedures.
quick.risks: Researchers note mirrored composites can create artificial features, and natural expression adds temporary asymmetry. Press coverage has linked appearance-rating practices to body dysmorphia concerns.

angle.text: Users reverse a face photo or compare its two halves to assess symmetry, one of several features in facial analysis, then target asymmetries or choose angles. Symmetry features in attractiveness research; this self-test itself has not been validated.

facial-analysis-youtube-channels.summary: Creators break down and rate faces on feature scales like PSL, showing viewers which of their features to improve and how.

quick.overview:
Facial analysis channels are creators who assess faces on video or livestream, rating features such as eye tilt, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like PSL. Viewers use them to learn where their face stands and what to change.

The chain: creators rate eyes, jaw and cheeks, viewers learn which features hold their look back, then choose changes from skincare to surgery. The ratings are not scientifically validated, and critics call parts of the scale pseudoscientific. No studies have examined the content or its viewers.
quick.how: Viewers submit photos for review, follow breakdowns of their features and watch before-and-after comparisons. Creators assign a tier or score and suggest changes, which viewers pair with grooming, fitness, skincare or procedures.
quick.risks: Press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. Critics describe PSL-style ratings as pseudoscientific.

angle.text: Viewers watch creators rate faces on feature scales such as PSL to learn which features to improve and how. The ratings are not scientifically validated, and press coverage links the content to body-image concerns.

anti-looksmax-touch-grass-critiques.summary: The counter-discourse to looksmaxxing, from journalists and clinicians to the informal 'touch grass' nudge to log off and spend time offline.

quick.overview:
This entry covers criticism of looksmaxxing, from journalism, academic papers and clinicians to the casual 'touch grass' jab telling absorbed users to go outside.

The chain people describe: question the obsessive focus on looks, shift time to offline life and relationships, and gain confidence and social presence. Within the scene it is read as a counterweight to over-focus on looks, and the benefits it suggests are anecdotal. Wikipedia records criticism that the movement is judgmental, that mewing and bonesmashing are regarded as misinformation by doctors, that it relies on anecdote, and that it may channel young men toward incel views.
quick.how: It shows up as press and academic critique, replies on forums and social media, and friends or family nudging heavy users toward offline activity. Some practitioners combine looks work with limits on screen time and forum use.
quick.risks: No direct risks. The topic concerns reported harms such as body dysmorphia and injuries from practices like bonesmashing.

angle.text: Journalists, researchers and clinicians argue looksmaxxing can be harmful, while the informal 'touch grass' version urges absorbed users to go outside and spend more time offline. Within the scene it is read as a counterweight to over-focus on looks, and the benefits it suggests are anecdotal.

therapy-for-looks-related-anxiety-act.summary: A mindfulness-based talk therapy raised for appearance anxiety, to help it interfere less with daily life and social presence.

quick.overview:
Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) is a talk therapy that teaches people to notice thoughts and feelings, accept them rather than fight them, and act on personal values. In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a way to handle appearance anxiety so it holds back confidence less.

The chain: mindfulness and acceptance skills, less appearance-related anxiety running the show, then a calmer, more confident presence. ACT was developed by Steven C. Hayes in the 1980s, and the wider literature includes more than 1,000 randomized trials, with mixed findings against standard CBT. No study here tests it specifically for looks-related anxiety.
quick.how: People work with a trained therapist in regular sessions, using mindfulness and values exercises, and practise between sessions. Self-guided ACT books and apps also exist. Changes are described over weeks to months.
quick.risks: ACT is generally a low-risk talk therapy. Critics question whether its distinctive components drive its effects.

angle.text: Acceptance and commitment therapy is raised in looksmaxxing discussions as a way to handle appearance anxiety so it interferes less with daily life and social presence. ACT is well studied generally, though not within looksmaxxing.

antidepressants-anxiety-meds.summary: Prescription drugs for depression and anxiety that some people use to ease social anxiety and low mood, which can hold back confidence and presence.

quick.overview:
Antidepressants are prescription drugs used mainly for major depressive disorder and also for anxiety disorders such as generalized and social anxiety, panic disorder, OCD and PTSD. In the scene they come up as aids for anxiety or low mood that hold back confidence.

The chain: lower anxiety or low mood, easier social interaction, a more relaxed, confident presence. They are prescribed for mental-health conditions, not appearance, and no study tests them for looksmaxxing concerns. Meta-analyses find they beat placebo in depression by a modest margin; for anxiety disorders the effect size is about 0.3.
quick.how: They are prescribed by a clinician after assessment and taken as a regular daily course, often alongside talk therapy. Most act on serotonin, sometimes with norepinephrine, and effects build over weeks. Main classes include SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs.
quick.risks: Reported effects include sexual dysfunction, weight change and emotional blunting. An FDA warning covers suicidal thinking in people under 25, and stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms. Prescription only.

angle.text: Prescription antidepressants and anxiety medicines come up in the scene as aids for social anxiety and low mood that can hold back confidence, making interaction easier and presence more relaxed. They are prescribed for mental-health conditions rather than appearance.

psychedelic-therapy-for-self-image.summary: An experimental idea of using psilocybin, LSD or MDMA therapy to shift how you see your own appearance; the drugs are controlled substances.

quick.overview:
Psychedelic therapy is the use of drugs such as psilocybin, LSD and MDMA, with preparation and integration sessions, in mental health treatment. Some forum users float it as a way to reshape how they see their own appearance and gain self-acceptance and confidence.

The chain: guided psychedelic sessions, a shifted view of self-image, more self-acceptance. Research has focused on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use. The only body-image item is a 2024 review in which a single psilocybin dose given for OCD symptoms raised insight in patients who also had body dysmorphic disorder, leading them to seek treatment.
quick.how: Clinical use is in supervised sessions with preparation beforehand and integration afterward, generally within clinical trials. Outcomes are described as depending heavily on mindset and setting, and mechanisms are poorly understood.
quick.risks: The drugs are Schedule I in the US. Contraindications include psychosis history, pregnancy and SSRI use, and some medications and psychiatric histories rule it out.

angle.text: Some forum users float psilocybin, LSD or MDMA therapy as a way to reshape how they see their own appearance and reach more self-acceptance. Research has focused on depression, PTSD and anxiety, and no direct body-image studies exist.

social-media-dysmorphia-filter-dysmorphi.summary: Informal name for wanting to look like your filtered selfie, which drives interest in procedures and photo framing; studies link it to body dissatisfaction.

quick.overview:
Social media dysmorphia, also called filter or Snapchat dysmorphia, describes people who want to look like their filtered selfies. It drives interest in cosmetic procedures and in how photos are framed and edited. The term was coined by British surgeon Tijion Esho, who saw patients shift from bringing celebrity photos to edited images of themselves.

The chain: edit or filter selfies, wish to match the edited look, then seek procedures or change presentation. Filters smooth skin and reshape features in real time. Observational studies link photo editing and image-focused platform use to body dissatisfaction and willingness to consider surgery, though much of the evidence is correlational.
quick.how: People bring edited selfies to consultations, try filters before choosing procedures, or adjust lighting, angles and framing to get closer to the edited look. Clinicians discuss it alongside body dysmorphic disorder.
quick.risks: It is an informal term, not a diagnosis. Researchers link heavy editing and platform use to body preoccupation and surgery consideration, though causation is unproven. Surgeons are urged to screen for BDD, and cosmetic surgery is not considered a treatment for it.

angle.text: The term describes people who want to look like their filtered selfies, which drives interest in cosmetic procedures and in how photos are framed. Studies link filter use to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, though it is an informal term and not a formal diagnosis.

beauty-privilege-research-pretty-premium.summary: Economic research finding that better-looking people are hired and paid somewhat more, which looksmaxxers cite as a reason to invest in appearance.

quick.overview:
The pretty premium is the research finding that people rated more attractive tend to be hired more and paid more. Looksmaxxers cite it as a reason to invest in appearance. The landmark 1993 to 1994 study by Hamermesh and Biddle reported a plainness penalty of about 5 to 10 percent in earnings, somewhat larger than the beauty premium.

The chain: higher rated attractiveness, better hiring and pay outcomes, motivation to improve looks. Later résumé experiments in Argentina, Israel and Peru found callback advantages for attractive applicants, with patterns that differ by country and sex. Researchers propose halo-effect bias, employer or customer preferences, and productivity in interpersonal jobs; which applies is debated.
quick.how: People use it as a reason to prioritise grooming, fitness, skincare and style, particularly for interviews and customer-facing work. It is a body of findings rather than a practice.
quick.risks: No direct physical risk. Studies are observational or résumé experiments and do not show that specific looks changes raise earnings. Some jurisdictions, such as Belgium, have laws covering appearance-based discrimination.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers cite labour-economics findings that more attractive people tend to get better hiring and pay outcomes as a reason to invest in appearance. The premium is documented in research, while its size and causes are still debated.

evolutionary-psychology-of-attractivenes.summary: The theory that beauty preferences are evolved mate-choice adaptations, used to decide which features, like symmetry and dimorphism, to prioritise.

quick.overview:
Evolutionary psychologists propose that preferences for symmetry, averageness, sexual dimorphism and certain body ratios evolved because they signalled health, fertility or genetic quality. Looksmaxxers use the framework to decide which facial and body features to prioritise.

The chain: preferences are linked to health cues, which point to symmetry, averageness and dimorphism, which become targets for face and body changes. The idea is that natural and sexual selection shaped mate-choice mechanisms that respond to such cues. Support in research is mixed and contested.
quick.how: People use it as a checklist when assessing faces and physiques, then work on features such as jaw and brow structure, symmetry, leanness and shoulder-to-waist ratio through grooming, training or procedures.
quick.risks: No clinical risks apply. Critics within science note weak or inconsistent links between attractive features and health, cultural variation in preferences, and studies limited to narrow samples.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers draw on evolutionary accounts of beauty to decide which features, such as symmetry and sexual dimorphism, to prioritise for face and body changes. Support in research is mixed and contested.

spreader-grafts.summary: Cartilage strips placed beside the septum during rhinoplasty to keep the nose bridge straight and smooth after a hump is reduced.

quick.overview:
Spreader grafts are thin strips of cartilage, usually from the septum, placed along the nasal bridge during rhinoplasty. They keep the middle of the nose straight, hold the bridge lines smooth after a hump is reduced, and avoid a pinched mid-nose. They also widen the internal nasal valve.

The chain: cartilage strips beside the septum hold the upper lateral cartilages away from it, giving a straighter, supported bridge and a smooth profile. The result is visible once healed. Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and technique papers, with at least one registered randomized trial whose results were not found.
quick.how: Surgeons place them as part of a rhinoplasty, often when a dorsal hump is reduced, using cartilage taken from the patient's own septum. Some surgeons use techniques such as component dorsal reduction that lessen the need for them. Final results develop as swelling settles over months.
quick.risks: It carries general rhinoplasty risks, and revision rhinoplasty accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases. Graft-specific complication rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure performed only by clinicians.

angle.text: Surgeons place these cartilage strips during rhinoplasty to keep the middle of the nose straight and the bridge lines smooth after a hump is reduced. The reshaping is visible once healed; published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series.

columellar-strut-graft.summary: A hidden cartilage post under the nasal tip, placed during rhinoplasty to hold the tip firm and in a defined position.

quick.overview:
A columellar strut is a small cartilage graft placed between the medial crura in the columella during rhinoplasty to support the nasal tip. It is hidden under the skin and invisible after healing.

The chain: a concealed cartilage post gives a firmer, supported tip, which helps hold tip shape and position. Surgeons have long assumed it increases tip projection, and a retrospective review of 100 consecutive primary rhinoplasties examined its effect on projection and rotation. Surgeons also compare it with the caudal septal extension graft, which some describe as offering more control of tip position.
quick.how: It is done as part of a rhinoplasty, using the patient's own cartilage. Many surgeons now also use septal extension grafts. The tip's final shape settles as swelling resolves over months.
quick.risks: Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general, and revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. Graft-specific rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure.

angle.text: Rhinoplasty patients get this concealed cartilage post to hold the nasal tip firm and in a defined position. The change is visible after healing, though surgeons debate how much it raises the tip compared with septal extension grafts.
